promptText: Why do classical exact structures like k-d trees fail as an index for text embedding search?
options: K-d trees can only store integers, not floating-point vectors

As dimensionality grows into the hundreds or thousands (typical of text embeddings), the curse of dimensionality collapses the tree's pruning power, degenerating into checking almost the entire dataset
K-d trees require a GPU to operate correctly
K-d trees can only be used with the Euclidean distance metric
explanation: K-d trees and similar spatial trees work well in low dimensions but their pruning power collapses in high-dimensional spaces (the curse of dimensionality) -- text embeddings typically live in 384 to 4096 dimensions, well past where these structures remain useful.

promptText: What does 'approximate' mean in Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search, and why is it an acceptable trade-off?
options: It means results are randomly selected without regard to similarity
It means the index does not guarantee finding the mathematically exact top-k neighbors, trading a small, tunable chance of missing some true neighbors for dramatically faster query times
It means the vectors themselves are stored with reduced precision at all times
It means the search only works for datasets under 1,000 vectors
explanation: Exact nearest-neighbor search over millions of high-dimensional vectors is computationally infeasible at interactive latency; ANN indexes deliberately accept a small, controllable chance of missing a true neighbor in exchange for orders-of-magnitude speedup.

promptText: What does recall@k measure for a vector index?
options: The number of queries per second the index can sustain
The fraction of the true top-k nearest neighbors that the approximate index actually returns, compared against exact search as ground truth
The percentage of vectors that pass a minimum similarity threshold
The amount of memory the index consumes per stored vector
explanation: Recall@k is computed by comparing what an ANN index returns against the true top-k neighbors found via exact (flat) search; it is the standard metric for how much accuracy an ANN index is sacrificing for speed.

promptText: At a high level, how does HNSW answer a query faster than brute-force comparison?
options: It compresses all vectors to a single bit before comparison

It builds a multi-layer graph with sparse, long-range connections at the top and dense, short-range connections at the bottom, and greedily narrows the search from sparse to dense layers instead of comparing against every vector
It deletes vectors that are rarely queried to shrink the search space over time
It only searches vectors inserted within the last 24 hours
explanation: HNSW's layered graph lets a query skip across large portions of the dataset via sparse top layers before refining through denser lower layers, making comparisons scale close to logarithmically with dataset size instead of linearly.

promptText: In IVF (Inverted File Index), what role does the `nprobe` parameter play?
options: It sets the total number of vectors stored in the index
It controls how many of the nearest clusters (centroids) are actually searched at query time, trading recall against latency
It determines the embedding model's output dimensionality
It sets how many replicas of the index are created for high availability
explanation: IVF clusters vectors around centroids at build time; nprobe controls how many of the nearest clusters get brute-force searched at query time -- more probes means higher recall but higher latency.

promptText: What happens if you query a vector index using a distance metric different from what the embedding model was trained/evaluated with (e.g., Euclidean instead of cosine)?
options: The query is automatically rejected with a clear error message
The query still runs and returns results that 'look plausible,' but rankings can be silently degraded in ways that are hard to detect without a recall benchmark
The vector database automatically converts the metric to the correct one
The embedding model recomputes all vectors using the new metric on the fly
explanation: A mismatched distance metric does not throw an error -- it silently returns a plausible-looking but potentially incorrect ranking, which is why this bug is notoriously hard to spot without benchmarking against ground truth.

promptText: Compare IVF and HNSW. In which scenario would you specifically prefer IVF (typically paired with Product Quantization) over HNSW?
options: When you need the absolute best recall at any memory cost
When the dataset is so large that raw memory footprint, not recall or insert latency, is the binding constraint
When the data changes very frequently and needs graceful incremental inserts
When you need zero index build time before the first query
explanation: HNSW generally achieves better recall at comparable latency and handles incremental inserts more gracefully, but consumes more memory per vector; IVF combined with Product Quantization becomes the better choice when memory footprint at massive scale is the dominant constraint.

promptText: Why does filtering results after an ANN search runs (rather than during it) risk returning far fewer than k results, or none, for a heavily filtered tenant?
options: Post-hoc filtering is always mathematically equivalent to filtering during search

If most of the raw top-k candidates happen to belong to other tenants, filtering them out afterward can leave very few or zero usable results, even though matching results exist elsewhere in the index
Post-hoc filtering only fails when the vector database has fewer than 100 total vectors
This only happens when cosine similarity is used instead of Euclidean distance
explanation: Running ANN search first and filtering afterward can silently starve a heavily-filtered query of results if the unfiltered top-k happens to be dominated by other tenants; the fix is pushing the filter into the graph/cluster traversal itself.

promptText: What trade-off does Product Quantization (PQ) make when paired with an IVF index?
options: It increases both memory usage and accuracy simultaneously with no downside
It compresses stored vectors into small codes, trading a small amount of accuracy for a dramatic reduction in memory footprint at large scale
It eliminates the need for a distance metric entirely
It only works with binary embeddings, never floating-point ones
explanation: PQ splits vectors into sub-vectors and replaces each with the ID of its nearest learned codeword, dramatically shrinking memory usage at the cost of some accuracy -- critical once storing tens of millions of high-dimensional vectors in RAM.

promptText: In HNSW, what do the parameters M and efSearch each control?
options: M controls the number of shards; efSearch controls replication factor

M controls how many edges each node keeps per layer (affecting recall and memory); efSearch controls how wide the candidate list is kept during a query's greedy walk (affecting recall and query latency)
M and efSearch are the same parameter under two different names
M controls the embedding dimensionality; efSearch controls the distance metric used
explanation: M is a build-time parameter governing graph connectivity (more edges = better recall, more memory); efSearch is a query-time parameter governing candidate list width (wider = better recall, higher latency).

promptText: An ANN index configuration that gave 98% recall at 100,000 vectors silently degrades to 80% recall after the collection grows to 10 million vectors, with no errors thrown. Why does this happen?
options: The vector database automatically corrupts data once it exceeds 1 million entries

Index parameters like efSearch or nprobe that were tuned (or defaulted) for the smaller collection are not automatically re-validated as the collection scales, and recall degradation is a silent, statistical failure mode rather than an exception
This indicates a hardware failure in the underlying storage
Recall always stays constant regardless of collection size for any ANN index
explanation: ANN index parameters are tuned relative to data scale; as a collection grows dramatically, the same efSearch/nprobe values can produce meaningfully worse recall without throwing any error, since nothing crashes -- retrieval just quietly gets worse.

promptText: Why is 'embedding inversion risk' a real security consideration for vector databases, even though vectors look like meaningless numbers?
options: Embedding vectors are always encrypted by default, so this is not actually a risk

Research has shown embedding vectors can, under some conditions, be partially reconstructed back toward the original text, so stored embeddings of sensitive documents may warrant the same access controls as the source content
Embedding inversion only applies to image embeddings, never text
This risk is eliminated automatically once vectors are normalized to unit length
explanation: Because embeddings can potentially be partially inverted to recover original text under some conditions, they should not be assumed to be inherently anonymous or safe to co-mingle -- the same access control and encryption practices applied to source documents should extend to their embeddings.

promptText: A RAG application's answer quality visibly worsens after its knowledge base grows from 500K to 20M chunks, with no code changes and no errors in the logs. What is the most likely root cause and correct diagnostic first step?
options: Immediately swap to a different vector database vendor without further investigation

Run a recall@k benchmark comparing the current ANN index's results against flat/brute-force search on a query sample; the likely cause is that efSearch/nprobe were tuned for the smaller collection and never revisited after a 40x scale increase
Assume the embedding model has been silently replaced by the provider and file a support ticket
Increase topK in every query until the problem disappears
explanation: Since there are no errors, this is a silent quality regression; benchmarking recall against exact search first confirms whether the ANN index's parameters, left untuned since the collection was far smaller, are now producing degraded recall at the new scale.

promptText: Why is cross-tenant data leakage through inadequate filtering considered especially dangerous in a vector database compared to a typical authorization bug?
options: It is not actually dangerous since vectors cannot be traced back to their source tenant

The failure is silent -- a similarity search without a correctly enforced tenant filter returns another tenant's semantically close chunks as a plausible-looking, valid result with no error, so it can go undetected far longer than a typical authorization bug
Vector databases are immune to cross-tenant leakage by design
This risk only exists when using IVF indexes, never HNSW
explanation: Because embeddings are opaque numbers, an unfiltered or poorly filtered search returning another tenant's chunks looks like a normal, plausible result rather than an obvious error -- making this class of leak far harder to detect than a typical authorization failure.

promptText: A platform team is designing a multi-tenant RAG system expected to scale to hundreds of millions of vectors across thousands of tenants, with a mix of a few huge tenants and many tiny ones. What is the key trade-off in choosing between per-tenant shards and a shared, filtered index?
options: There is no meaningful trade-off; a shared index is always strictly better regardless of tenant size distribution

Per-tenant shards give strong isolation and predictably small, fast per-tenant indexes but create heavy operational overhead managing thousands of small indexes; a shared, filtered index is operationally simpler but pushes the filtered-ANN correctness problem front and center
Per-tenant shards eliminate the need for any distance metric configuration
A shared index cannot support metadata filtering under any circumstances
explanation: The sharding decision trades operational simplicity against isolation and index size predictability: per-tenant shards isolate cleanly but multiply operational burden, while a shared index is simpler to run but requires first-class filtered ANN support to remain correct and fast for every tenant.
